# Embed as a Go library

openrate is a Go library first. The JSON API and the web console are one
optional layer on top of it, not the only way in. Four packages, each paying
for only what it uses:

| Package | What it is | Touches the network? |
|---|---|---|
| [`fx`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/vul-os/openrate/fx) | the pure core — graph, snapshot, accuracy model, `Describe` | never |
| [`fxsource`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/vul-os/openrate/fxsource) | the `Source` interface, the adapters, and the only `os.Getenv` in the module | only when a `Source.Fetch` is called |
| `openrate` (this package) | `Engine` (computes) and `Refresher` (fetches) | only if you build a `Refresher` |
| [`serve`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/vul-os/openrate/serve) | the optional HTTP shell and the optional web console | never on its own — it answers from an `Engine` it does not own |

Import `github.com/vul-os/openrate` for `Engine` and `Refresher`. Add `serve`
only if the program should also speak HTTP.

```bash
go get github.com/vul-os/openrate
```

Two runnable programs — one importing the package, one driving a sidecar over
loopback — are in [`sdks/go/`](https://github.com/vul-os/openrate/blob/main/sdks/go/README.md); `bash sdks/go/examples/run.sh`
runs both. Everything on this page applies to the first of them. **Go is the
one language with no FFI story at all**: no shared library, no `dlopen`, no
platform matrix, none of the costs on [the C ABI page](#c-abi). If your
program is not Go, that page and the
[fifteen language packages](https://github.com/vul-os/openrate/blob/main/sdks/README.md) are where to start instead.

## The headline case: an Engine with no Refresher

This is the case that answers the real objection to embedding an FX engine in
a program that only sometimes needs one: **can I construct it behind a feature
flag that is off and be sure the process is unchanged?**

```go
import "github.com/vul-os/openrate"

e := openrate.NewEngine(openrate.EngineOptions{Base: "ZAR"})

c, err := e.Convert("USD", "ZAR", 100)
// err is ErrUnknownPair: the engine holds an empty snapshot and has never
// been fed one. No goroutine started, no socket opened, no environment
// variable read, no packet sent — not during NewEngine, and not during
// Convert, which only ever reads the snapshot it already has.
```

`NewEngine` starts nothing. It materializes an *empty* snapshot so every read
method works immediately instead of having to special-case a nil, and it
answers every question honestly with "I don't know" (`ErrUnknownPair`,
`ErrUnknownBase`) rather than a zero. A host can build one unconditionally,
gate the rest of the FX feature behind a flag, and know the flag being off
means the engine never does anything more than exist.

## Feeding it without a Refresher

An `Engine` does not care where its rates come from. `Load` installs a
snapshot built any way you like — from a file, a cache, another process — with
zero network calls of openrate's own:

```go
import (
	"time"

	"github.com/vul-os/openrate"
	"github.com/vul-os/openrate/fx"
)

e := openrate.NewEngine(openrate.EngineOptions{})

g := fx.NewGraph()
g.Replace("mysource", []fx.Edge{
	{From: "USD", To: "ZAR", Rate: 18.50, Source: "mysource", Time: time.Now()},
})
e.Load(g.Materialize(time.Now().UTC()))

c, err := e.Convert("USD", "ZAR", 100) // now answers from what you gave it
```

`Load` is also what a `Refresher` calls internally — there is nothing a
`Refresher` can do to an `Engine` that your own code cannot do the same way.

## `Engine`

`EngineOptions`'s zero value is valid: base `ZAR`, `slog.Default()`, the real
clock.

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Base` | `string` | `"ZAR"` | Default presentation base currency. Every method still takes the currencies it operates on explicitly. |
| `Logger` | `*slog.Logger` | `slog.Default()` | Pass `slog.New(slog.DiscardHandler)` for silence. |
| `Now` | `func() time.Time` | `time.Now` | Inject a fixed clock in a test for byte-identical answers on every run. |

| Method | Description |
|---|---|
| `DefaultBase() string` | The presentation base the engine was configured with. |
| `Snapshot() *fx.Snapshot` | The immutable all-pairs view currently being answered from. Never nil. |
| `Load(snap *fx.Snapshot)` | Installs a snapshot, replacing whatever the engine held. A nil snapshot is ignored. |
| `Convert(from, to string, amount float64) (Conversion, error)` | The full provenance for one conversion — arithmetic, path, sources, age, grade. |
| `Rates(base string) (map[string]fx.Pair, error)` | Every currency against `base`. An engine with no rates yet returns an empty map and no error — "nothing yet" is a readiness question, not a bad request. |

All methods are safe for concurrent use.

## `Refresher` — the only thing that touches the network

A `Refresher` fetches from `fxsource.Source`s and feeds the results into an
`Engine`. It is the one type in this module that opens a socket, and
constructing one still does nothing until you call `Refresh` or `Run`:

```go
import (
	"context"

	"github.com/vul-os/openrate"
	"github.com/vul-os/openrate/fxsource"
)

e := openrate.NewEngine(openrate.EngineOptions{})
r := openrate.NewRefresher(e, openrate.RefreshOptions{
	Sources: fxsource.Build("ecb,coinbase"),
})

ctx := context.Background()
go r.Run(ctx) // or: r.Refresh(ctx) once, on your own schedule (cron, a request, a boot hook)

if err := r.Ready(ctx); err != nil {
	// ctx was cancelled before any snapshot with a currency in it arrived
}

c, err := e.Convert("USD", "ZAR", 100)
```

`RefreshOptions`:

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Sources` | `[]fxsource.Source` | — (required) | What to fetch from. No default: a `Refresher` exists to fetch, and *what* it fetches has to be the caller's decision, never an environment variable's. |
| `Interval` | `time.Duration` | `1h` (`DefaultRefreshInterval`) | How often `Run` refreshes. Ignored by `Refresh`. |
| `FetchTimeout` | `time.Duration` | `50s` (`DefaultFetchTimeout`) | Bounds each individual source fetch — generous because the SARB host can take tens of seconds just to connect. |
| `Logger` | `*slog.Logger` | `slog.Default()` | One warning per failed source fetch. |

| Method | Description |
|---|---|
| `Refresh(ctx context.Context) error` | Fetches every source once, concurrently, and loads the result. Synchronous: it returns once the Engine holds everything this attempt could get. Returns an error only when *nothing* could be fetched — every source failed, or `Sources` was empty (`ErrNoSources`). A source that fails keeps its previous edges; the rest of the snapshot is unaffected. |
| `Run(ctx context.Context) error` | Refreshes immediately, then on `Interval` until `ctx` is cancelled. Blocking — `go r.Run(ctx)` is the caller's choice, not this method's. Returns `ctx.Err()` on cancellation; a single tick failing does not stop the loop. |
| `Status() []SourceStatus` | Per-source fetch outcomes, in configuration order — what `/api/v1/meta` reports over HTTP. |
| `Ready(ctx context.Context) error` | Blocks until the `Engine` holds a snapshot with at least one currency, or `ctx` is done. |

### Why `Ready(ctx)` and not "the health endpoint answered"

`NewEngine` materializes an *empty* snapshot immediately, so a process can be
up, serving, and answering `ErrUnknownPair` on everything for however long the
first fetch takes. `Start`'s old contract — wait for `/healthz` to return
200 — only ever proved the listener was accepting connections, never that a
rate existed. `Ready` is the signal that was missing: it blocks on the engine
actually holding data, not on the process being alive. It does not itself
fetch — something else has to be refreshing, or `Ready` simply waits for a
snapshot that will never arrive.

## Sources: `Build` vs `FromEnv`

```go
fxsource.Build("ecb,coinbase")  // pure: same spec, same set, on every machine
fxsource.FromEnv()              // OPENRATE_SOURCES, plus any paid source whose key env var is set
fxsource.FromEnvSpec(spec)      // like FromEnv, but the spec comes from you (e.g. a flag), not OPENRATE_SOURCES
```

`Build` is the library call: given the same string it returns the same
sources, so nothing about a host's environment can silently widen what it
fetches from. `FromEnv`/`FromEnvSpec` are the explicit opt-in to environment
configuration — the `.env`-and-it-just-works path `cmd/openrate` uses. Nothing
else in `openrate`, `fx`, or `serve` reads the environment; `fxsource` is where
that one `os.Getenv` lives, and only `FromEnv`/`FromEnvSpec` call it.

## Serving over HTTP (optional)

`serve` answers HTTP requests from an `Engine` it does not own and cannot
refresh — importing it adds no outbound capability, only an inbound one you
have to wire up yourself:

```go
import (
	"net/http"

	"github.com/vul-os/openrate/serve"
)

api := serve.New(e, serve.Options{
	UI:     true,        // mount the console at "/"; off by default
	Status: r.Status,    // powers /api/v1/meta's source-status field
})

http.ListenAndServe(":8080", api.Handler())
```

`serve.New` starts nothing, binds nothing, fetches nothing. `Handler()`
returns the full standalone handler (routes plus rate limiting, security
headers, `robots.txt`); `Routes(mux)` mounts just the routes on a mux you
already own, if openrate is one API among several in a larger program. See
[the API reference](#api) for what gets served and
[serve.Options](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/vul-os/openrate/serve#Options)
for the rest of the fields (`CORSOrigin`, `RateLimit`, `TrustedProxies`).

## The `noui` build tag

The web console (`serve/web/ui.html`, plus a bundled copy of
`THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt`) is compiled in by default and is what `UI: true`
mounts. Building with `-tags noui` removes the embed from the binary entirely
— not just from what gets served — and swaps in a small JSON stub that answers
the same paths. Measured in this checkout, on the default `cmd/openrate`
build:

| Build | Size |
|---|---|
| default | 10,035,714 bytes |
| `-tags noui` | 9,969,458 bytes |
| **saving** | **66,256 bytes (≈ 65 KiB)** — `serve/web/ui.html` (40,287 bytes) plus its bundled `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt` (25,298 bytes) |

The more useful fact for an embedder, though, is what happens when you never
import `serve` at all — or import it but never call `Handler`/`Routes`.
Building a few one-file test programs against this checkout with `go build`
(default flags, no `-ldflags`, go1.25, darwin/arm64):

| Host program | Size |
|---|---|
| empty `main` (no openrate import) | 2,371,362 bytes |
| imports `fx` only | 2,476,034 bytes |
| imports `fxsource` (adapters, incl. `net/http`+TLS) | 6,740,770 bytes |
| imports `openrate`, calls only `NewEngine` — never `serve`, never the deprecated `Start` | 7,115,330 bytes |
| also imports `serve`, actually calls `.Handler()` with `UI: true` | 7,644,786 bytes |

Two things fall out of that table. First, `fx`→`fxsource` is where most of the
weight is (≈4.3 MB), and it is `net/http`/`crypto/tls`, not the sources
themselves — near-zero marginal cost inside a host that already speaks HTTP.
Second, and this is the one worth trusting: the engine-only host above
contains **zero** bytes of the console (verified by grepping the binary for a
CSS class string that only exists in `ui.html` — zero matches). Go's linker
drops `Handler` and the data it embeds when nothing reachable from `main`
calls it. A program that imports `openrate` for `NewEngine`/`NewRefresher` and
never touches `serve` does not pay for the console at all, whether or not
`-tags noui` is set — the tag only matters to a program that *does* import
`serve`.

## Deprecated: `openrate.Start`

`Start` is the original embedding path: it binds a loopback listener, launches
a refresh loop, and starts fetching from the network — all before it returns,
none of it optional. That is exactly backwards for a library whose whole point
is that constructing it should be free.

```go
// Before:
local, err := openrate.Start(openrate.Options{})
if err != nil {
	log.Fatal(err)
}
defer local.Close()
resp, _ := http.Get(local.APIBaseURL() + "/rates")

// After — the same three decisions, made explicitly instead of bundled:
e := openrate.NewEngine(openrate.EngineOptions{})
r := openrate.NewRefresher(e, openrate.RefreshOptions{Sources: fxsource.FromEnv()})
go r.Run(ctx)

api := serve.New(e, serve.Options{Status: r.Status})
srv := &http.Server{Addr: ":8080", Handler: api.Handler()}
go srv.ListenAndServe()
```

`Start` keeps working — it is built on exactly these three pieces internally
— so nothing that depends on it breaks. New code should reach for `NewEngine`
first and add `NewRefresher`/`serve.New` only when it actually needs to fetch
or serve.
